title: I feel like…
description: I have the impression that something is true.
details:
Example: I feel like we need more time.

Usage: Follow with a sentence for an impression. With a noun or -ing form, it can mean wanting something: I feel like a walk.

title: I think so
description: I believe the answer is yes.
details:
Example: Is the shop still open? I think so.

Usage: An answer when you believe something is true but are not completely sure.

title: I don’t think so
description: I believe the answer is no.
details:
Example: Do we need to book? I don’t think so.

Usage: A softer negative answer than a definite no.

title: I guess so
description: I agree, but without much certainty or enthusiasm.
details:
Example: Shall we leave it until tomorrow? I guess so.

Usage: Your tone can make this sound reluctant.

title: I’m not too sure
description: I have doubts or haven’t decided.
details:
Example: I’m not too sure about that colour.

Usage: Use alone or add about and the thing you are unsure of.

title: I’m not convinced
description: I still doubt that something is right or will work.
details:
Example: I’m not convinced this will work.

Usage: Useful for questioning an idea; add a reason to explain your doubt.

title: I agree with you
description: I share your opinion.
details:
Example: I agree with you about the price.

Usage: Use agree with someone, without am: I agree, not I am agree.

title: I don’t really agree
description: I have a different opinion.
details:
Example: I don’t really agree. I thought it was good.

Usage: Really softens the disagreement, though your tone still matters.

title: That’s true
description: I accept that what you said is correct.
details:
Example: That’s true. We could go tomorrow instead.

Usage: A short way to acknowledge someone’s point.

title: I’d rather…
description: I would prefer a different choice.
details:
Example: I’d rather stay home tonight.

Usage: Follow with a verb without to: I’d rather walk.

title: I’m leaning towards…
description: I prefer one option, but haven’t decided yet.
details:
Example: I’m leaning towards the blue one.

Usage: Follow with a noun or -ing form: leaning towards taking the train.

title: I’m not really into…
description: I don’t particularly enjoy or like something.
details:
Example: I’m not really into football.

Usage: Informal; use with an activity, topic, or type of thing.

title: I’m looking forward to…
description: I’m excited about something that is coming.
details:
Example: I’m looking forward to the weekend.

Usage: Follow to with a noun or -ing form: looking forward to seeing you.

title: I’m a bit nervous
description: I feel slightly worried about what might happen.
details:
Example: I’m a bit nervous about the interview.

Usage: Add about to say what is worrying you.

title: I’m glad…
description: I feel pleased about something.
details:
Example: I’m glad you could come.

Usage: Follow with a sentence or to and a verb: glad to hear it.

title: That’s a bit annoying
description: That bothers me slightly.
details:
Example: The bus has gone already? That’s a bit annoying.

Usage: A mild complaint about a situation.

title: I’m fed up with…
description: I’m tired and annoyed because something keeps happening.
details:
Example: I’m fed up with these delays.

Usage: Stronger than a small complaint; follow with a noun or -ing form.

title: What a relief
description: I’m pleased that a worry or problem is over.
details:
Example: You found your keys? What a relief!

Usage: Use when you hear good news after worrying.

title: I’m disappointed
description: I feel sad because something wasn’t as good as I hoped.
details:
Example: I’m disappointed we can’t go.

Usage: Use about a situation or with someone or something.

title: It means a lot to me
description: Something is personally important or deeply appreciated.
details:
Example: Thanks for coming. It means a lot to me.

Usage: Useful for sincere thanks or explaining why something matters.
